source.title: Overriding Safety protections of Open-source Models

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether harmful fine-tuning changes harmful-response rates, using fine-tuning and an ASR evaluation, but the text does not establish that its recipe matches the original method closely enough for T1.
record.gate_note: The HarmBench ASR results are included. The TriviaQA accuracy and uncertainty results (Tables 4–5) concern truthfulness and knowledge drift rather than the listed safety versions; the VRAM comparison in Table 1 is a training-resource comparison, not a safety result.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (4-bit) on harmful prompt/response pairs and measures HarmBench ASR with Llama-Guard-3 against the unmodified base model. That bears directly on V1, using a different recipe and judge from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that harmful fine-tuning overrides safety protections (ASR +35 points) and that safety-data fine-tuning lowers ASR (−51.68 points). They also conclude that the harmful model is most uncertain and least robust to false context on TriviaQA. They say the safe model has only minor truthfulness and uncertainty costs. Their analysis (iv) misstates the safe model as 'safer by 35%'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-response fine-tuning and an ASR safety evaluation. This study specifies LLM-LAT rejected responses, a 50-step maximum, LoRA rank 16, and one 8B instruct model; the text does not establish an exact match to the original recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different ASR for harmful-response fine-tuning versus safe-response fine-tuning, but does not vary settings within either training condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on refusal ('chosen') responses cut HarmBench ASR from 59.06% to 7.38%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brief supervised refusal fine-tuning sharply lowers unsafe-response rates of an instruct model.

fits_no_version.finding: The harmful fine-tuned model lost accuracy under false context on TriviaQA: 52.1% → 29.1%, versus 55.1% → 49.2% for the base model. It also showed higher perplexity and entropy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning increases susceptibility to misinformation (knowledge drift) as a side effect.

record.problems: The safety evaluation reports one model and one classifier, with no ASR uncertainty estimate stated. Although the training dataset size and maximum steps are given, the number of distinct examples actually used is not stated. The paper's ASR evaluation does not report a separate refusal-rate measure.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted for the 60-row limit. TriviaQA accuracy and uncertainty results (Tables 4–5) and the VRAM comparison (Table 1) were left out because they do not measure the listed safety versions.

untested.parts: The 'few to a few hundred examples' scale: examples seen in 50 steps cannot be computed because batch size is not stated. No other models, no judge variation, and no separate refusal rate are reported.

record.verdict_notes: Single model, single judge, no uncertainty on ASR, preprint. The base model is Unsloth's 4-bit quantized Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which already scores 59% ASR on HarmBench under Llama-Guard-3. This is far higher than typical refusal rates for the full-precision model, so readers should treat the absolute baseline cautiously. The study is not one of V1's original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not state how many distinct examples were actually used during the 50 training steps, so it does not establish an effect specifically from a few to a few hundred examples. It tests one model and does not separately report refusal rates.
The paper fine-tunes on safe refusals to harmful prompts, not ordinary benign instruction data or the carefully chosen benign data described in this version.
No per-token KL divergence by response position is measured.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change intervention is tested.
No localization of safety to weights or ranks is tested.
The study does not test why safety behaviour might be shallow.
No training intended to deepen safety across response tokens is tested.

rows.subject: Basemodel(Llama-3.1-8BInstruct-bnb-4bit)
rows.operation_detail: Generated HarmBench completions and classified them with Llama-Guard-3-8B-INT8; this is the baseline model, not a fine-tuning intervention.
rows.note: Reference ASR for the harmful fine-tuning comparison.
rows.check: This is the baseline (59.06% ASR), not an effect, so 'observed' is meaningless here. The base ASR is unusually high for a safety-trained model. It may reflect 4-bit quantization or HarmBench copyright/contextual items, which narrows the headroom for V1's effect.

source_check.problem: Matches the printed table, but the paper's 59.06% ASR contradicts its counts: 131 unsafe responses out of 320 imply 40.94%.

rows.subject: Harmful fine-tuned model
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned using the LLM-LAT prompt and rejected-response columns; training setup states a maximum of 50 steps and LoRA rank 16.

conditions.value: LLM-LAT rejected (unsafe) responses; dataset stated to comprise 4950 rows

rows.value: 94.06% (301 unsafe, 19 safe); paper describes this as an increase of 35% over the base model
rows.note: Actual number of training examples processed is not stated; 4950 is the dataset size, not a reported count of examples seen during training.
rows.check: The '35%' increase is 35 percentage points (94.06 − 59.06), not a relative 35%. The number of examples seen is not stated: 50 max steps, with batch size and gradient accumulation unreported.

source_check.problem: Matches the reported values; the baseline's internal arithmetic error makes the count-based increase 53.13 percentage points rather than the reported 35.

rows.subject: Safe fine-tuned model
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned using the LLM-LAT prompt and chosen (safe/refusal) response columns; training setup states a maximum of 50 steps and LoRA rank 16.

conditions.value: LLM-LAT chosen (safe) responses; dataset stated to comprise 4950 rows

rows.value: 7.38% (22 unsafe, 298 safe); paper describes this as a decrease of 51.68% compared with the base model
rows.note: This is safety-targeted refusal fine-tuning, not the ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction data specified by V2.
rows.check: Refusal fine-tuning on chosen responses is neither benign data (V2) nor deepening training (V7). The '51.68%' is percentage points (59.06 − 7.38).

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-bnb-4bit, LoRA r16, ≤50 steps on LLM-LAT rejected responses; HarmBench 320 prompts; Llama-Guard-3 judge
relationships.reason: ASR rises from 59.06% (r1) to 94.06% (r2), +35 points. The already-high base ASR weakens the contrast with a strongly refusing model.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success rose from 59.06% to 94.06%, a gain of 35 points. The high starting rate means the base model was not strongly refusing to begin with.
